1:
The word that opens the section is not what the English suggests. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) says outright that the Greek means not finally but furthermore, what remains; Ellicott (grammatical-historical) renders it for the rest, the same formula that opens the practical part of the earlier letter at 1 Thessalonians 4:1. Gill (reformed) marks what the section is for: discipline, and the removing of the disorderly. Ellicott quotes Chrysostom — he had prayed for them, and now asks their prayers — and observes how much of a teacher’s power comes from the accumulated intercession of his own converts. Henry (puritan-evangelical) makes it a doctrine of fellowship: praying for one another in absence keeps up the communion of saints, so that men far apart meet at the throne of grace, and those capable of no other kindness may do and receive a great one. Calvin (reformed) adds the qualification that matters: Paul surpassed others in prayer and still did not despise theirs, and what he asks is not personal but the gospel’s progress.

What he asks for the word gets a metaphor and a distinction. Ellicott takes may have free course literally as may run along, hearing speed and security in it. Robertson (grammatical-historical) notes both verbs stand in the present, so the sense is may keep on running and being glorified, a pairing found nowhere else in the New Testament; he traces the figure to the stadium and relays Lightfoot’s rendering, a triumphant career. Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) glosses it as going on swiftly and being owned divine. Calvin separates the two verbs: the first is dissemination and advancement, the second something further, that the preaching should have power to renew men after the image of God, so that the holiness of Christians is what glorifies the word.

Then the men who obstruct it, where one Greek adjective divides four witnesses. Barnes (grammatical-historical) traces it from out of place through absurd to improper, concluding it points less to malice than to misplacement. Clarke reads it as disorderly and unmanageable, men under no discipline. Ellicott goes the other way, from misplaced to extravagant and monstrous, illustrating from the dying thief at Luke 23:41, who said Christ had done nothing so monstrous as to deserve it. Robertson lists the range: odd, unbecoming, perverse, outrageous. On who is meant Gill offers the unbelieving Jews or the false teachers; Calvin takes both, then names Chrysostom as restricting it to those who opposed the gospel by false doctrine rather than violence — for his part extending it to every kind of danger, Paul being then bound for Jerusalem under the forewarning of Acts 20:23.

The clause about faith turns on a word Clarke will not translate as the others do. He argues it means fidelity rather than belief, pointing to the next verse where the Lord is called faithful by the same root: many who have received some divine light are still men we cannot confide in. Robertson keeps the ordinary sense and makes their conduct follow from lacking it; Wesley agrees. The Lord’s faithfulness is where Chrysostom (eastern-antiochene) sets the balance of the passage. Having committed everything to the prayers of the saints we ought not to be idle, nor when working good to despise that help; prayer effects great things, but when we also work. So the promise to stablish and guard is at once followed by the confidence that they will obey, lest thinking the whole to be of God they should sleep. He promised to save and will save, but as he promised: if we are willing and hear him, not like stocks and stones. Gill and Barnes take the verse as comfort against the discouragement before it, and Clarke adds that the evil they are kept from may be read the evil one.
6:
Here the letter turns to discipline, and Gill (reformed) is careful about who is addressed. The command goes to the brethren, the whole society, not the officers alone: the executive power of receiving and excluding lies with the elders, the power of judgment with the church. Barnes (grammatical-historical) supplies the history. Paul had raised this in the earlier letter in the mild language of exhortation, backed by his own example, and neither worked; so the language becomes command, with the church required to withdraw from those who will not labour. What first made them idle, he says, is not known. Henry (puritan-evangelical) draws the general lesson first: the best society of Christians may have faulty persons in it, perfection not being had on this side heaven — but evil manners beget good laws, and the disorders at Thessalonica produced rules of constant use since. On the phrase in the name of the Lord the two grammarians part. Robertson (grammatical-historical) takes the name for authority. Ellicott (grammatical-historical) takes it literally, as naming the name aloud in the act, the way a miracle is done in the name of the Lord.

What counts as walking disorderly is the question underneath the command. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) and Robertson both work from the military figure of men out of their rank; Robertson notes the verb means to break the ranks of soldiers, and that Paul denies the charge of himself in the same word. Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) narrows it to the point at issue: disorderly particularly by not working. Calvin (reformed) makes the narrowing explicit: the word is not applied to men of dissolute life but to indolent persons employed in no useful occupation, and that, he says, is what disorder really is. He describes them as idle and at once inquisitive and talkative, drifting from house to house to scrape a living at others’ expense, and forbids that their indolence be encouraged by indulgence.

The tradition they departed from is disputed in a small way with a large edge. Clarke insists it means the orders of the first epistle and nothing else: no unwritten word, no uncertain saying handed from man to man, but part of a revelation they could find in a letter. Wesley says it covered both, the admonition given by word of mouth and the one in writing. Ellicott answers a related question against Chrysostom, who made the tradition consist of example without precept: the compressed phrase means they had received both, a rule and a model. Robertson calls the demand for imitation daring, explaining it by Paul’s need to set new converts a pattern.

The waiver of his rights draws the strongest agreement in the chapter. Gill says Paul preserved the claim even while not using it, lest ministers who could not support themselves be injured by the example, and lest covetous men turn it against ministerial maintenance generally. Clarke and Ellicott both prefer authority or right to the word power, Ellicott adding how jealously Paul guards the rights of the apostolate — not for himself, but for others and for the future. Robertson notes that Paul did accept help where it could not be misread. Calvin calls the moderation singular and sets it against men who abuse their powers so as to infringe their brethren’s rights, likening the idle to drones that make no honey and live on the honey of others. On the maxim itself all agree Paul did not invent it: Barnes finds it current among the Jews and the same sentiment in Greek writers, and Clarke calls it a proverb which universal nature teaches, founded on the sentence of Genesis 3:19 — adding that it is a sin to relieve merely artificial necessities. Barnes narrows the application: what is refused is support at the public expense.
11:
How the news reached Paul is guessed at. Barnes (grammatical-historical) says plainly that it is not known who brought it; Ellicott (grammatical-historical) supposes the bearers of the first letter carried word back; Gill (reformed) notes that a man with the care of all the churches kept up a correspondence by messenger and letter. What was reported turns on a pun three witnesses notice independently. Ellicott calls it a scornful play on words lost in English, the term for busybodies being a compound of the term for working; Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) calls it a fine paronomasia, evidently intended; Robertson (grammatical-historical) renders it doing nothing but doing around, preferring Ellicott’s version, doing no business but being busy bodies. Ellicott hears something in the phrase among you too: not simply that some walk disorderly, but the vague directions of aimless feet going house to house.

On what such men are like the descriptions sharpen. Clarke lets himself go: impertinent meddlers, newsmongers and telltales, an abominable race and the curse of the neighbourhood. Barnes explains the mechanism more coolly, that men with no business of their own take up other men’s. Robertson calls them theological dead-beats, too pious to work and willing to eat at their neighbours’ expense. Calvin (reformed) draws the longest line, taking these drones for the seed of idle monkhood: men had made free with other tables under a pretext of religion from the beginning, and by Augustine’s day had grown numerous enough that he wrote a book against them, complaining, as Calvin reports, that they pleaded infirmity and yet wished to seem holier than others for being exempt from labour.

The remedy is put twice over. Ellicott notes that the severe verb appears for the fourth time in the chapter and might be rendered we order, but that Paul at once softens it with an entreaty resting on their union in Christ; Robertson says the same, that Paul asserts authority as an apostle and pleads as a man. On working with quietness Clarke is brisk, less noise and more work; Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) puts it as letting other people’s concerns alone. Calvin makes the deeper point, that the most peaceable men are those busy in a lawful calling, while those with nothing to do trouble themselves as much as others. Ellicott presses the words their own bread further: they need not exclude a common purse, since bread earned for a community would still be the workers’ own. Barnes then warns of a danger nobody else names: the idle discourage charity toward the deserving, until, unable to tell one applicant from another, we close our hands against all. The word for being weary, he adds, properly means to turn coward.

Then the sentence, with a construction dispute inside it: whether by this epistle belongs with the disobedience or with the marking, so that the church is told either to note the man who disobeys this letter, or to report him by letter. Barnes keeps the first, the church needing no help to identify the case; Ellicott agrees and rules the alternative out on the article; Clarke reports the second without adopting it. Calvin assumes the reporting, and thinks Paul meant to repress such men by his own authority before ordering excommunication — grounding the severity on the point that refusing this command is rebellion against God and not against a man. Robertson glosses the marking from the papyri, where the verb signs a receipt: tag that man. Then the limit. Barnes says this shows the spirit of all discipline, the standing danger being that we forget the offender is a brother and treat him as an adversary. Clarke turns it round: count him more an enemy to himself than to you, and labour for his soul. Wesley marks the boundary — no intimacy, no familiarity, no needless correspondence.
16:
The closing prayer is not detached from what precedes it. Calvin (reformed) ties them together: having forbidden the church to treat even the obstinate as enemies, and required that admonition aim at bringing them back, Paul could fitly add an injunction to cultivate peace — but since concord is a work truly divine he turns it into a prayer instead, which nevertheless carries the force of a precept. He suggests a second object as well, that God should restrain the unruly from disturbing the church at all. Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reaches the same connection by way of Chrysostom (eastern-antiochene), who saw the danger of quarrels breaking out over the very discipline just prescribed; and he adds that the busybodies’ conduct was destructive of peace in itself, for their own souls and for the community. The words by all means then widen it, in Ellicott’s reading, across everything the letter has treated: peace in every shape and form, through persecution and out of it, and through the terrors the earlier chapter described.

Who is asked for it, and what is asked, both get attention. Ellicott and Robertson (grammatical-historical) both notice that the first letter closed with the God of peace and this one with the Lord of peace, at 1 Thessalonians 5:23; Robertson takes it of the Lord Jesus, whose characteristic is peace and who alone can give the real thing to a heart or to the world. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) names him from Isaiah 9:6 as the Prince of peace and the fountain of it; Gill (reformed) as the author of peace in all his churches, who calls for it and encourages it; Barnes (grammatical-historical) simply as the one who alone can impart it. Henry (puritan-evangelical) unfolds what is being asked: peace with God, peace in their own consciences, peace among themselves, and peace with all men, and asked for always and in everything. He reads by all means as by every method — that having the means of grace they should use all the means of peace too, since peace is often difficult and always desirable. Clarke reports a textual variant here worth knowing: several manuscripts, versions and fathers read not in every way but in every place, which would make the prayer that God grant them prosperity always and everywhere.

The last thing Paul does is take the pen. Gill and Clarke agree on the practice: an amanuensis wrote the body, whether from dictation or as a fair copy, and Paul added the salutation in his own hand, which is what authenticated the letter. Clarke says why such a measure would be necessary, if forged epistles were being carried about; Robertson says the same more bluntly, that spurious letters already existed as 2 Thessalonians 2:2 shows, and that the signature let each church know the letter was his — ending on a wish, that the autograph copy might be found. Barnes understands the token to be some known mark or manner of signing, recognisable to the readers. Ellicott makes a finer distinction than the others. What Paul calls the token is the autograph addition itself and not the particular words it uses; the actual salutation does not begin until the benediction of the next verse, and this verse exists to draw attention to that one. He also faces the question the practice raises, that it seems scarcely credible anyone should have dared write a letter under an apostle’s name — and answers that the first epistle, whatever its claim, had not yet acquired among the Thessalonians the sanctity it carries now.
